content: Based on the available evidence and expert opinions, the World Health Organization (WHO) has developed new recommendations regarding sedentary behavior for adults living with chronic conditions. These recommendations are informed by evidence extrapolated from studies that included adults over 65 years of age and individuals with chronic conditions such as cancer survivors, hypertension, and type-2 diabetes. For individuals living with HIV, no evidence suggests that the health impacts of sedentary behavior would differ from those observed in the general population. However, due to the indirect nature of the evidence, the level of certainty was downgraded. The benefits of engaging in moderateto vigorous-intensity physical activity to counteract the risks associated with high levels of sedentary behavior were also considered. This evidence was extrapolated to inform recommendations for adults with chronic conditions, although the certainty of the evidence was downgraded due to its indirectness. The WHO Guideline Development Group (GDG) concluded that evidence on sedentary behavior in the general adult population could be applied to inform recommendations for cancer survivors, individuals with hypertension, type-2 diabetes, and HIV. The benefits of reducing sedentary behavior outweigh the potential harms for these populations. For children and adolescents (aged 5–17 years) and adults (aged 18 years and older) living with disabilities, many of the health benefits of physical activity observed in the general population also apply. Additional benefits for individuals with disabilities include improved cognition in those with conditions affecting cognitive function (e.g., ADHD) and enhanced physical function in children with intellectual disabilities. It is recommended that children and adolescents with disabilities engage in at least 60 minutes of moderateto vigorous-intensity aerobic physical activity daily, with vigorous-intensity activities and muscleand bone-strengthening exercises included at least three times per week. Adults with disabilities should aim for 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity weekly, along with muscle-strengthening activities on two or more days per week. Older adults with disabilities are encouraged to include multicomponent physical activities emphasizing balance and strength training at least three days per week to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls. If individuals are unable to meet these recommendations, any amount of physical activity is better than none, and they should gradually increase the frequency, intensity, and duration of activity over time. For individuals with specific conditions, such as multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, Parkinson’s disease, stroke, major depression, schizophrenia, and intellectual disabilities, physical activity has been shown to improve physical function, cognition, and quality of life. For example, individuals with multiple sclerosis benefit from improved mobility, strength, and balance, while those with Parkinson’s disease experience better motor function and cognitive outcomes. Similarly, physical activity can enhance walking function and reduce shoulder pain in individuals with spinal cord injuries. The GDG emphasized that the benefits of physical activity for individuals with disabilities far outweigh the potential risks. While sedentary behavior is unavoidable for some populations, such as wheelchair users, limiting sedentary time and replacing it with physical activity of any intensity provides significant health benefits. The evidence on sedentary behavior in the general population was extrapolated to inform recommendations for individuals with disabilities, recognizing that the physiological health benefits of reducing sedentary behavior are likely to be similar. The WHO guidelines stress that doing some physical activity is better than doing none. Individuals who are not currently meeting the recommendations should start with small amounts of activity and gradually increase over time. The GDG concluded that the benefits of physical activity and reducing sedentary behavior outweigh the potential harms, even for individuals with disabilities or chronic conditions.
